articles.title: New facility at Washington national lab will give researchers free access to automated tools
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: A first-of-its-kind autonomous research facility is taking shape in central Washington that will provide free access to scientists studying bacteria, yeast and other microorganisms.

The Department of Energy’s Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) broke ground on the lab, which will open in 2029. PNNL leaders said it will be “one of the world’s largest and most fully autonomous biosciences laboratories” and the first to offer public access through a competitive application process open to U.S. universities, companies and other national laboratories.
The Microbial Molecular Phenotyping Capability (M2PC) is a 30,800-square-foot expansion of the existing Environmental Molecular Sciences Laboratory on PNNL’s Richland campus.

The new facility will include an integrated system of more than 100 automated instruments that can be programmed to perform laborious research tasks, including growing microbes, measuring their growth and behavior, and linking their genetics and cellular functions to observable traits. Ginkgo Bioworks is supplying the devices.

“M2PC will bring together PNNL’s strengths in microbial science, automation and computing to dramatically accelerate our understanding of what microbes can do and how we put those capabilities to work,” PNNL Director Deb Gracio said in a statement.

The research could address challenges in human health, manufacturing, threat detection, food production and energy. M2PC will also contribute to PNNL’s effort to build computer models that predict and program the behavior of living systems.

The project is part of DOE’s Genesis Mission, which aims to modernize U.S. science through AI and automation. It is funded through the DOE Office of Science’s Biological and Environmental Research program.

articles.title: Watching fruit ripen pays off: Seattle ag-tech startup Strella lands $4.25M
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Seattle-based ag-tech startup Strella has landed $4.25 million to expand the reach of its technology that monitors produce to prevent spoilage and food waste.
The investment extends the company’s Series A round and brings its total funding to $26.25 million.
CEO and co-founder Katherine Sizov launched the startup in Philadelphia in 2019 and relocated its headquarters to Seattle four years ago to be closer to Washington’s fruit orchards.

Strella uses IoT devices to measure gases including ethylene, a plant hormone released by ripening fruit, and machine vision to monitor the produce. Its software interprets the fruit’s real-time conditions alongside data such as country of origin, packing date and varietal type.
The 19-person team serves customers in 26 countries and provides information to growers of apples, pears, avocados and citrus. It recently added kiwifruit to the lineup.
“Our vision is to become the system of record for quality in the food supply chain, or the ‘guardian angels’ of produce as it passes from hand to hand,” Sizov said.
The company works with all of the players in the supply chain, including farmers, produce packers, shippers, distributors and retailers.
“The next step for us is to begin stitching all the pieces together to become a one-stop shop for quality and tackle the food waste problem at scale,” Sizov said.

The United Nations estimates that roughly 33% of food intended for humans worldwide is lost or wasted, totaling $940 billion in annual economic losses. Waste in the U.S. is even worse, at about 40% of edible food and $218 billion each year.
The funding was led by SilverBlue , with participation by LeVert Ventures , Beta Milouot and PeakBridge .

articles.title: Icertis veterans reunite as AI startup HumanTronik acquires tech consultancy CloudMoyo
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: HumanTronik, an AI startup co-founded by Icertis co-founder Monish Darda, has acquired CloudMoyo , the Bellevue tech services firm that Darda helped spin out of Icertis in 2015.

The deal keeps two of CloudMoyo’s co-founders in charge: Darda, as CEO of its new parent company, and Manish Kedia, who continues to run CloudMoyo day to day. The family of the late Samir Bodas , CloudMoyo’s other co-founder and the longtime CEO of Icertis, sold its stake in CloudMoyo as part of the transaction, Kedia said.

Darda co-founded HumanTronik earlier this year with Singapore-based investor and early Icertis backer Kabir Narang. The company is developing what it calls “human language models,” its phrase for AI that learns how specific executives make decisions and work with others. Those models power AI agents inside Microsoft Outlook, Teams and other workplace software.

Financial terms of the deal weren’t disclosed. CloudMoyo, as part of HumanTronik, will keep its name and existing customer contracts, and will sell and implement HumanTronik’s technology in addition to its existing lines of business.

The business model: Kedia calls the approach “Service as Software.” Customers pay for software, he said, with ongoing support from CloudMoyo built into the subscription. Pricing is shifting from per-user fees toward fees based on results.

It’s part of a broader blurring of the lines between software and services across the industry, including the rise of forward-deployed engineers who work inside customers’ businesses to put AI to use.

CloudMoyo has more than 300 consultants. Over the past two years, its work has expanded from mostly implementing Icertis contract software to building AI tools on Microsoft’s Fabric data platform, for customers including Seattle-based Expeditors and Mexican railroad Ferromex. That AI business is growing at about 100%, outpacing the company’s more traditional work, Kedia said.

Kedia gave the example of a procurement director trying to cut spending by two points this year. HumanTronik’s agents would draw on conversations with suppliers and internal discussions, along with the company’s business data, to help the director and their team reach that goal.

How the deal came together: The acquisition moved quickly, Kedia said. He and Darda met in the Bay Area three to four months ago to talk about CloudMoyo’s AI work, and Darda showed him what HumanTronik was building. Negotiations took about two months.

Because Darda was a major shareholder in both companies and on the CloudMoyo board, he was not directly involved in the negotiations, according to Kedia, who noted that each side had its own legal counsel.
The founders have known one another for years, which made the talks easier, Kedia said. “We are staying within the families,” he said.

The Icertis connection: Darda co-founded Icertis with Bodas in 2009 and served as its CTO for about 17 years before stepping back in April to start HumanTronik. His title at Icertis is now chief mentor.
Kedia, who at one point led business development for Microsoft’s SQL Server database software, was president of Icertis for several months before leading the CloudMoyo spinout in 2015.

Icertis has no financial stake in HumanTronik or CloudMoyo, Kedia said, though the companies continue to work together. Icertis has been led by interim co-CEOs Rajat Bahri and Jim Moffatt since Anand Subbaraman departed in July, less than a year after succeeding Bodas. Bloomberg reported in February that Icertis was working with Goldman Sachs to explore a potential sale.
Narang led Icertis’s Series A funding round in 2015 while at Fidelity’s venture arm, Eight Roads, and later became a founding partner at B Capital.

Headquarters and headcount: HumanTronik is headquartered in San Francisco, where it plans to open an engineering center. Darda is based in Pune, India, where CloudMoyo has an engineering center, and HumanTronik is setting up a subsidiary in Singapore.

Nearly all of CloudMoyo’s employees are becoming HumanTronik employees, joining a few HumanTronik engineering leaders in the Bay Area, Kedia said. The combined company has about 20 people in the Seattle area, where CloudMoyo has had an office in Bellevue for the past decade. Kedia, who lives in the region, said the company plans to hire engineering, product and sales staff here.
That’s up from about 15 in 2016, when GeekWire last wrote about CloudMoyo . At the time, most of its roughly 200 employees were in Pune.

The name CloudMoyo came from a word the founders picked up while traveling: “moyo” means heart or spirit in Swahili. After the HumanTronik deal, Kedia said, the company’s new motto is “human with a heart.”

articles.title: Data farmers: Ag-tech startup Aigen grows AI-generated weeds to train its solar-powered farm robots
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: For years, Aigen has been building and tweaking solar-powered robots designed to pull weeds on farms. But the Redmond, Wash., startup is also raising a crop of its own: a growing, AI-generated collection of digital weeds and plants that teaches those robots what to pull.

That synthetic data, which Aigen calls Alchemy , is changing what the company can sell. Training its robots on a new crop used to require three to four years of collecting and labeling real-world images, co-founder and CTO Richard Wurden said. Now it takes about a week, helping Aigen attract growers of asparagus, hops, flowers, lettuce and more.

Wurden spoke with GeekWire by phone from FIRA USA, a three-day agricultural robotics expo at Yakima’s State Fair Park that wrapped up Thursday. He said Aigen made several sales at the show, including to growers it previously couldn’t serve.
“Now we’re saying yes to a bunch of crops, where previously we were locked into just doing a few,” he said.
Aigen is nearly sold out of robots for the 2027 season following the show, according to the company.

Aigen’s solar design is also getting more attention as fuel costs climb. U.S. diesel prices are up roughly 70% from a year ago, according to EIA data, and averaged nearly $6.30 a gallon this month, according to AAA . Many rival weed-control machines are pulled by diesel tractors, Wurden said, while Aigen’s robots run entirely on solar panels with a battery backup.
“It just so happens running a solar-powered robot without pesticides is the best possible timing right now,” he said.

Wurden and CEO Kenny Lee founded Aigen in 2020 after meeting in a climate-focused Slack group and discovering they lived about five minutes apart. Wurden, a mechanical engineer, previously worked on battery systems at Tesla and at Seattle electric boat maker Pure Watercraft. Lee is a cybersecurity veteran who co-founded Weblife.io, which Proofpoint acquired in 2017.
The mission is personal for both founders. Lee had non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma and Wurden has type 1 diabetes — diseases Wurden said have been linked to herbicide use.

The startup raised a $4 million seed round in 2022 and a $12 million round in 2023 led by ReGen Ventures, with participation from NEA and others. Wurden said the company has raised about $26 million in total. The startup now has about 15 employees.

Aigen’s Element robots are about 6 feet wide and topped with a roughly 400-watt solar panel. Cameras and AI distinguish weeds from crops, and mechanical arms pull the weeds out at the root. The robots cost $50,000 to $70,000 each depending on configuration, and Aigen typically sells them in packs of five, Wurden said.

Aigen has built more than 100 robots, all assembled in Redmond, and logged more than 15,000 hours in fields in California, Minnesota and North Dakota. Customers include organic soybean growers in North Dakota and tomato growers in California, Wurden said, and the company is expanding a recent pilot with an unnamed Fortune 500 company.
Alchemy has also become a product in its own right.

Large agribusinesses are using Aigen’s synthetic data, Wurden said. Because the plants are generated in simulation, each one comes perfectly labeled. That matters when weeds and crops overlap in ways that are hard to sort out from real photos, especially under shifting daylight. Aigen’s robots don’t use artificial lights. Wurden said the startup built the system out of necessity, because it couldn’t afford to pay people to label images by hand.
“Our AI now labels the data for us,” he said.
The company is choosy about who gets that data. Wurden said the company would work with precision-spraying companies that use less herbicide, but not with operations that broadcast-spray fields.

Next up: robots on Washington farms early next year, the company says. It’s also developing an orchard version with arms that reach out to weed between trees. And a next-generation robot is in the works.

Aigen is one of several Washington startups using AI to fight weeds. Issaquah-based TerraClear maps individual weeds so farmers’ existing sprayers hit only those spots. Seattle-based Carbon Robotics zaps weeds with lasers and trained its AI on 150 million labeled images of real plants. Aigen is betting synthetic data can teach its robots new crops faster.
Wurden said it’s refreshing to see technologists working on these problems rather than focusing on ad clicks or another gadget or service that may not be good for society.

“I support every company working on ag technology and things that help farmers, because farmers have felt like they’re left behind for a long time,” he said. “It’s a good way to cross the aisle in politics, too. Everybody needs food.”

articles.title: Downtown Highrise Project Still Under Fire as Design Gets Revised Taller
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The property owners behind a potential cross-laminated timber highrise project in Downtown Seattle aren't shirking away in response to considerable pushback against their project – they're going taller. Plans shown this week to the Seattle Landmarks Board would still add a residential tower above a retrofitted Doyle Building at 2nd Avenue and Pine Street, but include six more floors than a proposal initially floated last year .

That change is only likely to intensify opposition to the project, with preservation advocates wary of seeing significant changes to the landmarked 1920 structure joining forces with nearby condo owners not happy about seeing a new tower creep up next door. If built, the new structure would extend 23 stories up alongside its neighbor, the 39-story 1521 2nd Avenue building.

Fana Group, which owns the Doyle Building, has enlisted a team that calls itself Buildings Reimagined – made up of the design firm Clark/Barnes and general contractor BN Builders – to rethink the future of the four-story structure. The Doyle would be converted into a concrete structure capable of supporting a mass-timber tower above, retaining only the north and east facades. A one-story gasket level would accommodate the transition to 18 stories above.

Thanks to a 2025 change in state law , Washington cities can no longer require facade modulation or upper level setbacks with mass-timber developments projects or redevelopments that convert commercial space into residential. That means Seattle's existing tower spacing rules do not apply here, with an average distance to the 1521 2nd Avenue building of just under 21 feet. It also means that there are no variances being proposed by Clark/Barnes that could add additional red tape, with the landmarks approval process one of the only remaining barriers standing in the way of potential approval.

"By combining the preservation, the sustainable materials, innovative design, and construction talent, we're going to be able to add more housing downtown," W. Scott Clark of Clark/Barnes told the landmarks board Wednesday. "This is why we created Buildings Reimagined, to help distressed properties that are really challenged and also difficult to entitle, to demonstrate that preservation and financially viable development are not mutually exclusive, and that that they can benefit one another."

Historic preservation advocates apparently disagree. A group called "Save the Historic Doyle Landmark" has already sprouted up to oppose the project as presented, and the advocacy non-profit Historic Seattle sent out an action alert in advance of this week's meeting.

"While not a large or tall structure, the Doyle building has stood out through the decades as downtown has evolved, bearing witness to and surviving the boom-and-bust nature of this city. This human-scale, right-size, mixed-use building stands today due to its original high quality of design, construction, materials, condition, and integrity," Historic Seattle's email stated. "The proposal is to demolish most of the building, leaving only two facades standing, and erecting 23-stories of new residential construction behind the two facades. Let’s be clear. This is NOT an addition to a landmark. This is NOT adaptive reuse. This is NOT historic preservation. This IS facadism. If approved, this would be a demolition of most of the landmark."
But Clark pushed back on claims that they would be demolishing the Doyle this week, framing that as misinformation.

"We are not demolishing the building. We are keeping the two historic featured elevations on the two streets. [...] We are demolishing the alley facade and the roof, and we are going in and we're completely restructuring the interior of this building," Clark said. "Whether you're doing a one-story addition or a taller addition, you would need to reinforce the building to meet seismic. But given the loads that we're going to be subject to, we are going in and we're completely restructuring the internal of the building with a concrete structure."

One point of contention at the Landmarks Board is likely to be the massing of the upper story additions, which are only set back from the Doyle Building's cornices by about three-and-a-half feet. Multiple board members expressed concerns about this, especially as it relates to criteria set by the U.S. Secretary of the Interior on rehabilitation of historic structures. Criteria #9 states that new additions "will be differentiated from the old and will be compatible with the historic materials, features, size, scale and proportion, and massing" compared to the existing structure."

"What I've heard is that this has been scaled and designed to work with economics and making finances work. So as it stands, I have a lot of trouble supporting the project moving forward based on criteria number nine, and seeing that none of that has been applied to this project," board member Matthew Zinski said, referencing the gasket floor intended to be a break between the two segments of building. "Landmarks Board member Matthew Zinski said. "I struggle to see the design logic or what's being used there to help differentiate what's going on between the new addition and the existing building."
Clark defended the choice to extend the addition as far out as it's proposed, noting the limitations that are inherent on the site.

"I do have to say that we were dealing with the reality of a small [floor]plate. It's 8,900 square feet, and secondly, we had to deal with the condition of an eccentric core location, just given the overall dimensions and depths of the plate," Clark said. "We wanted to ensure that our unit layouts had the depth necessary to make comfortable living units, and so all of those things, all those very practical things, in conjunction with the vertical load path that we're trying to run through the building, in coordination with the structure, the existing structure of the landmark building really started to describe the overall mass and form of the building."
Board member Dan Sloat echoed concerns around the addition being too bulky.

"I really appreciate your discussion about the attempt to keep the the new tower structure visually quiet to create that contrast, and I think for me, the kind of equal proportioning of two parts fights against that a little bit," Sloat told Clark. "I'm having a hard time reading the visual quietness of the of the superstructure because it is so dimensionally similar to the structure below."

Wednesday's briefing, coming more than a year after the firm's first discussion with the Landmarks Board, still represents the early stages of the project. But the design team is heading toward applying for a Master Use Permit with the city, and is advancing forward. In the months ahead it will become clear just how much of an uphill battle getting final approval of the Landmarks Board will be.
But Clark clearly sees the project as a major benefit to downtown Seattle as a whole.

"[The Doyle building] really is at a crossroads, and we think what we're proposing is a very strong, responsible, and reasonable approach to revitalize the building and provide the needed housing downtown," Clark said.

articles.title: New murals bring street art veterans and local roots to five Pike/Pine walls
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Five new murals are now looking out over Pike/Pine, painted by a crew of street art veterans and underground culture builders putting their imprint directly onto Capitol Hill’s everyday walls.

Led by On the Block and the Seattle Artist Coalition for Equitable Development , the “Paint the Block” initiative pulls from “renowned street legends with local longevity and deep neighborhood roots” to turn neighborhood walls into community infrastructure.

The five works span high-traffic corners and quieter stretches. Along the wooden exterior of the Wildrose at 1021 E Pike, Takiyah “TDUB” Ward painted For Shelley, The Wildest Rose honoring the late co-owner of the ‘Rose and urging the neighborhood to “Stay Creative.”
At 1200 E Pine, Myron Curry wrapped the parking bay of NW Liquor in bold scenes of drinks and street life, aiming to “inspire and empower communities through impactful cultural art.”

On a brick wall at 1016 E Pike, project curator Carolyn Hitt joined Maurice “REESBO” Kennedy on Time Traveling , which Kennedy celebrated as a chance to tell their stories in their “own stomping grounds — Capitol Hill.”
A few blocks west at 1426 Boylston Ave, Gerardo “Periko” Peña added a mural of an oversized blue cat Mina lounging among bright red blossoms.

Across from Cal Anderson behind 1535 11th Ave, a massive double piece brings Sam Sneke back to where he says he first “cut my teeth doing graffiti on Capitol Hill” three decades ago, pairing his Welcome to Capitol Hill with Pine Legacy B by SPECSWIZARD , BeSo 206 , and Brandon “ArtbreakerBT” Thomas , all sealed under clear coats brushed on by hip-hop veteran Silas Blak .
Organizers say placing this work front and center sparks foot traffic and safety from the ground up.

“The Seattle underground and behind the scenes is vibrant,” Hitt said. “More resources to these vital culture pockets would go a long way to nurture extraordinary talents that are currently struggling to create under the crushing weight of our economic times.”
Funded by the Seattle Office of Arts and Culture’s HopeCorps under District 3 Councilmember Joy Hollingsworth , the effort is fiscally sponsored by Northwest Film Forum .

Hollingsworth secured $250,000 in JumpStart funds last fall to “support murals in and around Cal Anderson Park” through the HopeCorps program and another $25,000 to fund the painting of the park’s bathroom.
In this year’s budget debate, 19 Capitol Hill and Central District organizations and businesses have joined a call to move $8 million in budget from hiring more cops to spending more on artists.

The mural project also expands on years of DIY work on 11th Ave, growing out of monthly street markets and Eleven:Eleven , the all-ages “little campus of autonomous art studios” opened by On the Block founder Hitt.

Up next, Phase Two of the project will roll out an interactive mobile heritage map on the Capitol Hill Arts District site, followed by artist-led walking tours woven into regular Second Thursday Capitol Hill Art Walks and Second Saturday On the Block markets.

articles.title: Lefty Cheat Sheet: Election choices ‘beyond our two major newspapers’ — and some Seattle left on left political rassling
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The Lefty Cheat Sheet at leftycheatsheet.org has arrived as a practical civic utility built to solve one of Seattle’s biggest voter headaches:

Instead of acting like an editorial board that hands down a candidate slate and binary yes-or-no verdicts on ballot measures, the volunteer-run platform functions as an aggregator. Voters can review tracked endorsements across dozens of labor, housing, environmental, and transit advocacy groups, customizing weights and filters to match the specific causes they trust most.

Share The Cities , the group that developed the Lefty Cheat Sheet, describes itself as an all-volunteer Seattle grassroots collective focused on land use, transit, and housing justice and backed by modest community micro-donations. The nonprofit is led by educator and organizer Laura Loe and Kate Rubin, also the co-executive director at Be:Seattle , according to the city. UPDATE : Rubin tells CHS she is no longer part of the leadership of the group.

Naturally, launching an election resource in Seattle’s hyper-charged and robust political left ecosystem brought immediate friction. An independent PAC was blamed for weaponizing the guide in mass campaign texts while taking shots at The Stranger’s ownership changes , forcing the Lefty Cheat Sheet’s volunteer creators to publicly declare their independence. Around the same time, rival political consultants reportedly purchased the .com version of the address to possibly reroute web traffic toward a competing voter guide. UPDATE : One of the consultants involved tells CHS she intended the purchase as an “online joke” and did not intend to use it to redirect voters.
Digital arguments quickly flared over who was genuine and who was attempting to manipulate voters.

Even with the crossfire, the tool’s underlying premise seems like it could hold. Rather than relying on top-down decrees from legacy institutions or wading through endless social media spats, Seattle voters might have gained an adaptable way to more carefully decide their ballots.
You can find the cheat sheet at leftycheatsheet.org .
CHS reported here on the major issues Capitol Hill and Central District voters will decide on in November. You can find all CHS Election coverage at capitolhillseattle.com/tag/elections/
The General Election is Tuesday, November 3rd.

articles.title: Seattle councilmember proposes new rules to curb long-term budget deficits
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: As Seattle tries to tackle an estimated $175 million budget deficit, citywide Councilmember Dionne Foster has proposed two new fiscal sustainability measures designed to curb recurring, multi-year shortfalls.

The proposed legislation would establish accountability standards for both the executive and legislative branches at Seattle City Hall. Under the proposals, the mayor’s office would be mandated to submit balanced future-year financial plans for both the General Fund and the JumpStart Payroll Expense Tax Fund. In addition, the Seattle City Council would be required to ensure its final, adopted budgets maintain balanced projections over that same timeline.

The package builds upon voter-approved 2025 “Seattle Shield” legislation that cut B&O for small businesses, boosted taxes on large corporations like Amazon and Starbucks and required balanced out-year projections through 2030, but only applied that standard to the 2027 budget. Foster’s proposal aims to make multi-year fiscal discipline a permanent governing rule.

In her announcement, Foster said that the city can no longer balance its ledger year-to-year while leaving downstream deficits to future leaders. Fellow councilmembers Alexis Mercedes Rinck and Eddie Lin have voiced their support.
The council will review the proposals during budget briefings starting October 27th, with a public hearing on the 2027-2028 budget scheduled for November 5th.

articles.title: Mossback's Northwest: When Seattle Quakes
articles.author: Knute Berger
paras: On January 28,1700 large tsunami waves slashed a 500-mile stretch of the Island of Honshu, Japan. No earthquake was felt, but accounts of damage to villages by huge waves and, in one case, the wreck of ship were preserved in Japan’s written records. These suggested that somewhere in the Pacific a massive quake had occurred.

And it had, off the Northwest coast of North America two days earlier when the Juan de Fuca plate subduction zone ruptured and a massive 8.7 to 9.2 quake shook the region and altered the coastline from northern California to Vancouver Island with waves, flooding and landslides that drowned forests and destroyed Indigenous villages.

This is the “Big One” that experts are expecting to recur. Evidence suggests major Juan de Fuca quakes can happen at 300- to 900-year intervals. If you travel to the coast you’ll likely see signs indicating evacuation routes if a tsunami is on the way. Enjoy your stay!

There’s no doubt that another Big One would be devastating to the region, but on Puget Sound we’re a bit sheltered from a Juan de Fuca plate lollapalooza: the inner Salish Sea isn’t generally on the front lines of impact, and the Olympic mountains stand between Seattle and the Pacific coast. But we don’t need to look far for evidence of earthshaking changes here. We have faults of our own.

Notably, after much of Seattle was built, we found ourselves sitting on a previously unknown earthquake fault, the so-called Seattle Fault, that runs roughly from Hood Canal through south Seattle to Issaquah. Scientists only confirmed its existence in 1992.

The evidence of it included a still standing sunken forest in Lake Washington that slid off Mercer Island, and land on Bainbridge Island and West Seattle that had been lifted up between 20 and 30 feet. It generated a localized tsunami too. Testing revealed the quake that did that happened about 1,000 years ago. It changed the local landscape dramatically.

Those of us who live in and around Puget Sound know that the earth can shake periodically and create those moments of “where were you when the quake hit?” Like the 1949 quake, or the 1965 quake, or the 2001 Nisqually? By comparison to the Big One, these have been gentle reminders.

Long-timers all have memories of these. My father was a surgeon at Virginia Mason hospital in 1949 and remembered the quake hitting on April 13 near noon while he and another physician were scrubbing for surgery. The doc next to him jumped into the sink! Afterwards, my dad asked him why and his colleague replied that he’d been in the Philippines during a major quake and multi-story buildings fell down but left their plumbing standing, including sinks and toilets hanging from pipes in the air. The 1949 quake, centered between Olympia and Tacoma, did millions in damage and killed at least eight people. The 6.7 it was felt as far away as Montana.

Another rattled Seattle which hit at 8:29 am on April 29, 1965. I remember it vividly. I was at before-school orchestra practice at John Muir Elementary in south Seattle. The building shook, a friend dove under a table yelling “hit the dirt,” and our music teacher Mr. Bloom stood on his podium tuning a violin as if nothing was happening. I held my French horn above my head in case the ceiling fell in (it did crack). Interestingly, the old brick school was damaged and was eventually demolished and replaced.

The violent shaking in ‘65 impacted a live TV fashion show being broadcast from the Space Needle restaurant. This was a big test for the Needle whose consulting engineer, John Minasian, had insisted the tower’s design needed to be more earthquake-proof. One of the fashion models there that morning told me she was using a Needle elevator as a dressing room and as the Needle swayed she could see the ground 500 feet below between the elevator and the Needle’s floor. The tower swayed in a figure-eight pattern, as it was designed to do, and remained standing with only a few dishes broken and some nerves frayed.

One thing in common with our quakes: Pioneer Square takes a big hit. Much of it is built on landfill that can liquify when the ground shakes. But also, in the ‘49, ‘65, and the 2001 Nisqually, major fallout was in the form of falling bricks. Buildings come down, facades collapse, chimneys topple. When Seattle burned down in 1889, the business district was rebuilt of stone and brick. That helped solve the fire problem but revealed an earthquake issue.

I missed the 2001 Nisqually Quake—I was in California that day—but Mossback producer Michael McClinton did not. He has a souvenir from it: a bent menorah that leapt off athe shelf mantlepiece inof his office in the Odd Fellows building on Capitol Hill. Queen Anne home. The quake struck close to 11 am on Feb. 28. The 6.8 quake was centered in the south Sound. Brick buildings in Seattle were hit hard. One person died, some 400 were injured in the area. As someone who saw the quake as reported on CNN that day the footage made it seem as if the entire city of Seattle was in ruins. It was a relief to find out my home and family were safe, but the initial TV impression was of devastation. When I went to work for FEMA later that year, I learned that coverage was called “the CNN effect.”

But the quake had some expensive consequences. The Alaskan Way Viaduct along Seattle waterfront was damaged and that led to a multi-billion-dollar effort to replace it with a deep underground highway tunnel and a remaking of the seawall along Elliott Bay. In a way the Nisqually knocked the viaduct down without knocking it down but revealed its vulnerability. It too had largely been built on land fill.

No story about quakes in Seattle would be complete without mentioning the Beast Quake of 2011 when the Seahawks’ Marshawn Lynch ran for an incredible game-winning touchdown against the New Orleans Saints during a playoff game in SoDo, the crowd’s pounding excitement measuring on seismic registers as a mild earthquake. Similar readings have since been recorded by Mariners, Sounders and Taylor Swift fans.

articles.title: Idaho Lawmakers Tried to Conflate Abortion with Human Trafficking and Seattle Attorneys Are Fighting Back
articles.author: Megan Burbank
paras: Three years ago, the Idaho state legislature passed a law making it illegal to assist minors in crossing state lines to access abortion care. In the paranoiac tradition of American anti-abortion policy, the law was rooted in a poorly disguised moral panic : It specifically banned “abortion trafficking”—the fictional concept of shadowy adults coercing minors into having abortions and abducting them to make it happen. This, obviously, is a problem that doesn’t exist, and would curtail the very real rights of minors and their allies, all while claiming to have children’s best interests at heart.

Now, a lawsuit spearheaded by the Seattle-based gender equality legal advocacy group Legal Voice is challenging Idaho’s law, and what comes next could impact access to abortion everywhere, for better or for worse. “Everyone wants young people to be healthy and safe, but this law, if it stands, will put them in danger and isolate them from trusted adults, which is what nobody wants,” says Wendy Heipt, senior litigation counsel at Legal Voice.

Idaho has a trigger law that immediately criminalized abortion when Roe v. Wade was overturned, but Idahoans seeking abortions commonly travel to states like Washington and Oregon for care, a dynamic that predates Roe ’s reversal and has stymied the efforts of anti-abortion activists, since freedom of movement is a constitutionally protected right. But by targeting young people’s access to abortion, Idaho lawmakers may have identified a loophole in their efforts to curtail abortion-related travel, one likely to be replicated elsewhere if it’s allowed to continue.

Legal Voice is arguing that Idaho’s travel ban blocks the First Amendment by preventing Idahoans from even discussing abortions across state lines. The law is also poorly written: it states that it’s illegal for an adult to “harbor” or “recruit” minors, but doesn’t give clear definitions for either term, which creates confusion both about following and enforcing the law. And then there’s that one pesky detail in the Constitution: the right to travel between states is a fundamental personal freedom, one that states with anti-abortion policies have struggled to successfully undermine, even as restrictive abortion bans have gone into effect since Roe v. Wade was overturned.

In an April memorandum requesting a summary judgment in the case, attorneys from Legal Voice, the Lawyering Project, and Stoel Rives LLP mapped out concerns the law raises about barring travel tied to health care when that treatment is legal in the destination state. “If states could prohibit such assistance, the right to travel would become meaningless in practice,” they wrote.
But if Legal Voice’s case prevails, it could set a useful precedent by affirming that an anti-abortion policy in one state can’t necessarily be enforced in another.

So far, Legal Voice and the case plaintiffs have secured an injunction to keep the law from going into effect. It was modified following an appeal to the Ninth Circuit and remains partially in place. Still, according to Legal Voice, “Under the current order, our clients can still provide information, encouragement, and financial resources to youth seeking abortion care.” Now back at the district court level, both sides have issued motions for a summary judgment, meaning a ruling could soon be issued, without the need for a trial.

Legal Voice’s plaintiffs in the case are Lourdes Matsumoto, a lawyer who needs to freely share abortion information in her work with young survivors of sexual assault and domestic violence; the Northwest Abortion Access Fund; and the Indigenous Idaho Alliance, which works with five Northwest tribes and connects pregnant people with abortion resources. “They serve indigenous communities throughout Idaho, including for health care autonomy, and they want to support people making their own decisions, including minors,” says Heipt. “And their family structure doesn’t always fit the way the laws are written.”

In choosing to target young people and the adults who support them, Idaho’s law isn’t unusual. It’s a common tactic in anti-abortion legislation (and anti-trans legislation, for that matter; the two are irrevocably intertwined ): Work your way up to targeting access to health care for everyone, but begin by eroding minors’ access. “That’s typically where it starts,” says Heipt. “If they are successful with minors, I can assure you that it will not stop with minors.”

Historically, anti-abortion activists have accomplished this through policies like parental notification laws, popularized even before the US Supreme Court overturned Roe in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization . These laws required minors to involve their parents in decisions about abortion, or to make their case before a judge to get permission if involving a parent wasn’t possible.
Though it contains no real requirements for involvement from a caregiver, Idaho’s abortion travel ban has been justified, like parental notification laws, as a policy promoting parental rights.

But just as “abortion trafficking” isn’t a real problem, a parental rights framing around abortion doesn’t make much sense, either, since data shows most young people who seek abortion care voluntarily choose to involve trusted family members.

A study on parental involvement in minors’ abortion decisions, published in the Journal of Adolescent Health , found that most minors—64 percent—specifically shared their plans to seek abortion care with their mothers, and, intriguingly, that parental involvement did not automatically equate to greater confidence in pregnancy decisions. Even without parental support, 81 percent of young people had “high confidence” in their own decision-making around abortion; maternal involvement was “not significantly associated with having high confidence in the decision,” the researchers found.

This is a very different reality than the “abortion trafficking” Idaho’s travel ban has purported to solve. In fact, when the law was first introduced in the Idaho legislature, Idaho Anti-Trafficking Coalition executive director Jennifer Zielinski told the Idaho Statesman that conflating human trafficking with helping someone voluntarily seeking abortion disrupted actual efforts to stop trafficking and risked retraumatizing victims. While human trafficking does sometimes involve forced abortion or pregnancy as a tool of control, the Idaho law would do nothing to help. “It takes the true effort off course,” Zielinski told the paper.

Heipt agrees. “It really does a disservice to actual survivors of trafficking to call something ‘trafficking’ because you don’t like it,” she says. And even the bill’s proponents seemed to understand this: The word “trafficking” has since been removed from the law, a nod to its bad-faith framing.
Whether a judge will view it that way remains to be seen. A decision in the case is expected early next year.

paras: Train kills man in wheelchair: Moments before a BNSF freight train hurtled through a downtown Puyallup crossing, a couple in a car noticed a man in an electric wheelchair stuck trying to cross the tracks. A man jumped out of the car, tried to lift the wheelchair from the tracks, and, when that didn’t work, attempted to free the man from his seatbelt. The train came too fast. One year with the use of force tool: Last year, the Washington Data Exchange for Public Safety ( WADEPS ), a tool that tracks police use of force statewide, launched. If you’ve ever wanted to see how our police departments behave, now you can. This year, according to WADEPS, there have been 1,200 uses of force statewide. KING5 reports that these range from police “shootings to police releasing a police dog on a subject.” Eight people have died from use of force this year and there have been no officers disciplined. Only about 80 percent of the 218 departments in the state have their data represented here, though they’re all required to do so. Reports can also be inconsistent depending on the month.

Ballots discovered in Golden Gardens dumpster: King County Elections confirmed that two USPS bins full of ballots were tossed in a dumpster at Golden Gardens. They recovered 92 ballots and have reissued them to voters. The US Postal Inspection Service is investigating.

RIP Tom Skerritt: Seattle’s favorite actor, Tom Skerritt, known for playing Captain Dallas in Alien , an enlistee in M*A*S*H , and the sheriff from Picket Fences , died from natural causes Thursday. He was 93.

The weather: The sun keeps chasing away that rain that was in the forecast earlier this week. It will be mostly sunny today. Perhaps those rain drops will come this weekend, but I am afraid to promise anything.
Another Pacific Ocean hurricane: Hurricane Vance—no, not the vice president— is hurtling toward Mexico and could make landfall as a Category 3 storm.

Netanyahu ramps up West Bank operation after Israeli soldiers killed: Two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinians were killed in an exchange of fire in the West Bank. According to the Israel Defence Forces, two Palestinian assailants and an automatic rifle opened fire at a checkpoint near Hebron. Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claims this was an attempted terrorist attack. He’s now preparing a full closure of the West Bank and preparing to go house to house, seize weapons, and demolish houses. Human rights groups say Netanyahu is using the attack as an excuse to justify tougher measures against Palestinians ahead of Tuesday’s election where Netanyahu is on the ballot.
Oh, really? The White House reports that First Lady Melania Trump has brokered a cease-fire deal between Russia and Ukraine in the Ukrainian city of Oreshky.

Suspicious: Public Citizen, a nonprofit consumer advocacy group, wants answers . Last Saturday, during the No Kings March, Meta allegedly suspended the official No Kings Instagram account. Public Citizen has filed a Freedom of Information Act request to get to the bottom of the block.

Trump supports that terrible Ramaswamy ad: This week, Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy funded an attack ad on his Democrat opponent, Amy Acton. The ad features Acton’s estranged mother calling her a liar, saying Acton has “serious problems with the truth.” Acton has not seen her mother since 1978, when she testified against her stepfather for physically and sexually abusing her and her brother for years. She was 12. Many people—even Republicans—have denounced the ad, calling it a real low even for modern politics. Not Trump or his camp. Trump called it “powerful” and told Ramaswamy he should thank God for the ad.

German far-right party has been wooing Trump for a decade: Not to steal Hunter’s thunder, but here is some Nazi news. A data leak from the far-right German Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) shows efforts to court Trump and the MAGA movement starting a decade ago . Their closest line to Trump during his first presidency was through Steve Bannon. So far, during Trump 2.0, they’ve continued contact with those close to Trump.
A long read for your Friday: “ The Art of the Deal: Jared Kushner’s Hacked Phone Revealed His Secret Negotiations—Including More Than $700 Million in Transfers ”

Bird flu rages at Utah mink farm: Remember how bird flu has been ravaging American livestock for the past four years? But it’s been okay the disease can’t spread among humans and cause a devastating pandemic deadlier than COVID-19? Well, the flu has been ravaging a mink farm in Utah. Mink could be that intermediary host species that could incubate a bird flu mutation that ends up spreading to humans. The farm has not culled its mink. The state and federal government have been bungling the response to this infestation—and trying to keep it quiet. Read ProPublica’s report here .

Meanwhile, the measles outbreak continues. The US Centers for Disease Control reported that there were 4,588 cases in the country as of Thursday. Yet, the CDC has denied a request from Washington and California to validate a new “rapid, high-volume measles test in preparation for major outbreaks.” It denied the request due to “competing priorities.”
We’ll end on a song: My friends are getting married tomorrow. Congrats, John and Isabelle!

articles.title: UN peacekeepers prepare to exit Lebanon after 70 years – leaving behind a worrying security vacuum
articles.author:
<name>Mireille Rebeiz, Director of Dickinson Program in New Zealand, Dickinson College; University of Otago</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/mireille-rebeiz-1503505"/>
paras: For nearly 70 years, the blue helmets of United Nations’ peacekeepers have dotted the landscape of southern Lebanon. But those days may soon be over.
Under Israeli and American pressure, the U.N. Security Council unanimously voted in August to end the mandate establishing the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL .
It means the 7,565 members of UNIFIL deployed in Lebanon – representing about 46 countries – will depart the country no later than Dec. 31, 2026.

The end of the U.N. presence comes at a pivotal time. Israel and Lebanon have already held seven rounds of negotiations aimed at bringing a lasting peace to a region that has suffered from decades of conflict.

Brokered by the United States, these talks that led to the signing of the Trilateral Framework in June 2026 call for the disarmament of Hezbollah, the Israeli withdrawal from all Lebanese lands and the settlement of all disputes over borders. Yet all of these conditions are still some way off from completion – and beset by a series of barriers .

As such, the departure of the United Nations peacekeeping forces raises serious concerns. The potential for a security vacuum looms large in south Lebanon, especially given that Israel continues to bomb Lebanon despite a ceasefire that has nominally been in place since April 16, 2026 .

As a scholar of Middle East Studies , I know that UNIFIL has never been a permanent solution. But I fear that its termination creates more problems than it solves, especially when there are no clear replacements or post-UNIFIL security arrangements in place.
While the U.N. had had an on-the-ground presence in Lebanon to handle civil strife since the 1950s , its role in mediating between Lebanon and Israel started later.

In 1978, after a series of attacks on Israel organized by Palestinian fighters in Lebanon, Israel invaded and occupied the south in what was known as Operation Litani . As a result, the United Nations Security Council established UNIFIL to monitor Israel’s withdrawal from south Lebanon and to restore peace at the Lebanese–Israeli border.

Israel’s occupation of south Lebanon lasted more than two decades . Following its withdrawal on May 25, 2000, the U.N. set the Blue Line – a 75-mile (120 km) demarcation line created for the practical purpose of confirming Israeli withdrawal from south Lebanon. It was not an official border but a buffer zone monitored by the U.N. peacekeepers.
UNFIL and the Blue Line served as geographic and diplomatic focal points in the 2006 war between Hezbollah – an Iranian-backed militia operating from Lebanon – and Israel.

Resolution 1701 of the Security Council, which brought an end to the 2006 war, dramatically expanded the UNIFIL role in Lebanon ; the number of troops went from 2,000 to 15,000 authorized military personnel.

Its mandate also changed to include monitoring the ceasefire and documenting its violations, coordinating with Lebanon’s military and functioning as the only direct communication channel between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries. UNIFIL also offered humanitarian aid to the affected civilian population of south Lebanon.

Yet UNIFIL’s role never altered the basic lack of peace on the Israeli-Lebanese border. Over 50 years, Israel invaded Lebanon numerous times . And since 2000, Hezbollah has flourished in south Lebanon .

As UNIFIL prepares to depart, it’s unclear what will fill the looming security vacuum. It could be filled by non-U.N. troops, but Lebanon’s past shows the risks inherent to international peacekeeping missions.

In 1982, after Israel invaded Lebanon and occupied Beirut with the intention of eliminating the Palestinian militant threat, Lebanese authorities called on Western powers for help. In August, the governments of the U.S., France, Italy and the United Kingdom created a multinational peacekeeping force designed to restore peace and stop the fighting between the Lebanese, Palestinians and Israelis.
But on Oct. 23, 1983 , the multinational peacekeeping force was the target of a dual suicide attack that killed 241 American service members and 58 French paratroopers.
To this day, the attack – claimed by the pro-Iranian Islamic Jihad – remains the deadliest single-day incident for the U.S. Marine Corps since the Battle of Iwo Jima in 1945.
In addition to Israel, interventions in Lebanon have also come from another neighboring country.

In 1976, the Syrian military intervened during Lebanon’s civil war to put an end to sectarian violence. Nearly three decades of occupation followed, and troops were withdrawn only following the assassination of Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri in 2005 and the subsequent Cedar Revolution .
With the absence of an internal Lebanese consensus, the arrival of any international peacekeeping force to replace the exiting UNIFIL will be perceived by many Lebanese as a top-down imposition.

Moreover, the situation on the ground makes it dangerous for any international force to successfully operate. Israel is reportedly occupying over 10% of Lebanon’s territories , including multiple permanent bases and outposts in southern Lebanese territory.
Hezbollah, meanwhile, refuses to disarm .
Finally, the fate of Lebanon-Israel direct negotiations is unclear . Recently, the countries held military talks in Florida, but little is expected from them .

Yet a number of efforts are ongoing despite the difficult circumstances surrounding UNIFIL’s withdrawal. On June 25, French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced an “ international coalition to support Lebanon ” to reinforce Lebanon’s sovereignty and help prevent a security vacuum in south Lebanon.
In parallel, the European Union Foreign Ministers approved a new civilian-military mission aimed at advising and training the Lebanese military and police personnel.
But these appear to be limited operations that aren’t designed to replace UNIFIL.
U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has previously proposed that Syria enter Lebanon to help end the violence and execute “a surgical attack on Hezbollah.”
But given the past experience of Syrian occupation, this proposal would certainly not be welcomed by the Lebanese people.
Although Lebanese security is a paramount concern regarding the impending withdrawal of UNIFIL, it’s not the only potential risk.
UNIFIL employs many Lebanese civilians and is a steady consumer of local goods and services . It also provides humanitarian aid to the region.
And the departure of UNIFIL may further erode Lebanon sovereignty by opening the door for the sharing of security by neighbors – and former occupiers – Syria and Israel.

This is all the more worrying given that the Lebanese armed forces are poorly trained, have a poor record as a fighting force and will be susceptible to attacks from Hezbollah fighters and sympathizers, which might trigger sectarian violence in the country.
In the vacuum left by U.N. forces, some Lebanese military personnel might simply decide that opposing Hezbollah is too risky altogether.
All of these factors make what comes next for Lebanon after UNIFIL’s departure as opaque as it is worrying for those concerned about the country’s well-being.

For the sake of Lebanese sovereignty, the twin goals of disarming Hezbollah and ensuring Israel’s withdrawal from Lebanese territory remain paramount. Yet it’s unclear who will take on those duties absent a stronger Lebanese state.

For all of its inability to prevent wars, invasions and violations of ceasefires, UNIFIL’s presence guaranteed a degree of Lebanese sovereignty over its lands and served as a reminder of the international community’s commitment to peace in the region. An effective replacement force would at least have to do the same.
Mireille Rebeiz is affiliated with American Red Cross.

articles.title: PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat
articles.author:
<name>Doug Jacobson, University Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Iowa State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/doug-jacobson-809162"/>
paras: Governments and organizations around the world began scrambling on Oct. 21, 2026, to fix a vulnerability in software that runs their websites, a bug that could give hackers access to data and control of websites. The flaw in PHP, the programming language that powers much of today’s web, prompted urgent warnings from the U.S. National Security Agency , cybersecurity agencies and software vendors.

A researcher at Calif , a security research firm, found the flaw in August 2026 using an advanced artificial intelligence model from OpenAI. The firm alerted the nonprofit that manages PHP. However, word of the flaw leaked before the PHP organization released patches for its software, and according to Amazon Web Services officials, hackers began “broadly” attempting to exploit it .

The vulnerability has implications far beyond a single company or platform, because PHP is a key piece of software that helps run millions of websites. So, what is PHP, what role did AI play in uncovering the vulnerability, and should the average user worry?

PHP is a programming language that powers most websites . For a modern website to provide dynamic content, visual elements and searchable features, a program must run on the web server and take user input, whether that is entering a web address or clicking links and buttons. Estimates suggest that around 70% of websites run on PHP.

PHP operates on a web server in two main parts : the core PHP system – the engine and runtime libraries – and the individual PHP scripts, which are the custom programs that actually implement a website. When you interact with a website, PHP scripts run, take user input and produce the output your web browser displays.

The current security issue sits directly in the core PHP system and the libraries it uses. When a vulnerability exists at this deep level, it can allow an adversary to exploit the system. In this case, they can run unauthorized commands on the computer hosting the website, which allows attackers to access data and gain full control of the website.

This vulnerability is not a mistake in an individual website’s code. The issue lies in the core PHP system, making every unpatched system running PHP vulnerable. Since websites are accessible to anyone on the internet, adversaries can easily find PHP-based websites using automated tools. From there, they can run an exploit program that takes advantage of the vulnerability.

This exploit code is called PHP2Shell. This name comes from the fact that the exploit gives the attacker “shell access,” a cybersecurity term for direct command-line control of the computer running the website. Shell access bypasses the website interface, giving adversaries a window to enter commands and access all the website’s data.

What makes this vulnerability particularly interesting is how it was discovered. This exploit came to light through a process known as coordinated disclosure, in which cybersecurity researchers report the flaw to PHP developers before publicizing it.

This discovery shows the power of AI in cybersecurity. For decades, finding subtle software flaws required large teams of specialists manually reviewing code. Today’s AI systems can examine vast codebases and identify unusual patterns in hours or days. These models can analyze millions of lines of code in seconds, spotting subtle memory management bugs that human auditors might miss over decades of software development. The PHP vulnerability has existed in the core PHP code for over a decade, and AI helped researchers find it.

However, this also shows that attackers can use these same tools to locate and exploit vulnerabilities. The same reasoning capabilities that help security researchers find flaws first can also let attackers rapidly scan the web for vulnerable targets and automate the creation of tools to exploit the vulnerabilities.
This illustrates why it is so critical for security teams to use AI to find vulnerabilities and report them safely and actively. AI can also help release patches that mitigate these vulnerabilities .

Many government agencies, universities, hospitals and businesses rely on PHP-based systems . While individual internet users are unlikely to be directly affected, organizations that delay patching could expose sensitive data, risk having their operations disrupted or give attackers a foothold into larger networks.
PHP runs entirely on remote web servers. If you are an everyday internet user visiting websites, you do not need to download a patch or fix your personal computer.

However, if you manage a website, blog or server, even a small site built on popular content management systems such as WordPress, you should check your server administration panel or web host immediately to ensure your PHP software is updated to the latest patched version. If a third party hosts your website, check with them to see whether they have patched for these vulnerabilities.

The PHP2Shell discovery illustrates a new reality for cybersecurity. In our interconnected world, keeping web infrastructure secure is a continuous race. As AI tools become standard for both cyber defenders and online adversaries, maintaining fast patching habits remains our most essential defense.

articles.title: Why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway in Israeli politics
articles.author:
<name>Hannah Ridge, Assistant Professor of Political Science, Chapman University; Institute for Humane Studies</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/hannah-ridge-2473324"/>
paras: On Oct. 20, 2026, a week before Israel’s elections, dozens of men were detained on suspicion of evading the draft – arrests that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called “unacceptable .”

The young men attend ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, religious schools, whose students were long exempt from the military service mandatory for most Israelis. A 2024 court ruling that Haredi men must be drafted alongside other Jewish youth intensified the conscription debate. Netanyahu’s government has failed to either legalize the draft exemption or enforce the court’s ruling, though he has said Haredim who are not studying should enlist .

With Israel’s military fighting in several conflicts, those exemptions have become increasingly unpopular: The vast majority of Jewish voters want Haredi communities to share the burden . Haredi political parties, however, are key potential coalition members as Netanyahu attempts to secure his political future. Although a relatively small percentage of the population, the Haredim hold disproportionate sway in Israel’s parliamentary system.

Haredi Jews strictly observe Jewish religious law and often disapprove of liberal interpretations. They typically live in Haredi-majority neighborhoods where large families are the norm – six children, on average – and about half of the men devote themselves to full-time religious study . The poverty rate is 33% , more than double the percentage for non-Haredi Jews.

The Israeli public is about 14% Haredi , but the community is growing quickly because of its high birth rate. Projections by the Central Bureau of Statistics estimate that almost a quarter of Israelis will be Haredi by 2050.

Haredi communities are diverse and represented by two main political parties. Haredim who are Ashkenazi – Jews whose ancestors came from northern and eastern Europe – are linked to United Torah Judaism, or UTJ. Those who are Sephardi or Mizrachi, meaning their ancestors came from the Iberian Peninsula and the Middle East, are linked to Shas.

A third Haredi party, Haredi Public, was formed in July 2026 . The party says it will represent Haredim who feel underserved by Shas and UTJ , emphasizing employment and poverty, housing development and the education system. Unlike the other two Haredi parties, it has included women on its candidate list.

Elections for the Israeli parliament, the Knesset, use a proportional representation system . Any party that receives more than 3.25% of votes receives seats based on the fraction of votes it received. Each party allocates its seats to members based on a list of candidates published before elections.

Having multiple parties with similar target demographics risks dividing the vote, leaving that group with fewer representatives in the Knesset. Shas and UTJ have agreed to share their surplus votes in the 2026 election to maximize their overall seat share.

Because of the low electoral threshold, many parties are able to win seats. No Israeli party has ever attained the 50% share needed to control parliament by itself. As in other countries with similar systems, it is very common for parties to form coalitions and govern as a team.

Likud, one of the major conservative parties, has led most governing coalitions for the past two decades , with party leader Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister. Haredi parties are seen as strong conservative allies , and they have been key coalition members for Likud administrations. Today, as Netanyahu faces challenges from other right-wing parties over his handling of Oct. 7, 2023, and several wars, Likud may need them even more.
The fact that Likud has needed Haredi parties to form coalitions has given them negotiating power. For many years, one of their priorities has been draft exemptions for religious education .

Military service is mandatory for most groups in Israel, although Muslim and Christian Arab citizens are generally exempted. Jewish Israelis see conscription as a unifying experience and a costly demonstration of commitment to the state. Starting at age 18, most women serve two years and most men serve almost three years. Former soldiers can be called up as reservists into their 40s, depending on their training.

For decades, Haredi men received de facto exemptions. It was, effectively, one of several government arrangements that subsidize Haredi communities. Religious schools for teen boys and married men receive government payments for each student. Given the communities’ low employment rates, large families and high poverty rates, many families rely on public support .

In 2024, Israel’s Supreme Court ruled that a blanket exemption from military service for Haredim was not legal . Netanyahu’s government struggled to enact a compromise between those who favored drafting Haredim and the Haredi parties; the failure to find a lasting legal way to exempt Haredi men led Shas and UTJ to leave the Likud-led coalition in 2025.
Nonetheless, this ruling has not led to mass conscription.

Haredi groups have held public protests , and many have ignored draft notices. While tens of thousands of men are draft eligible but not serving , and most of them are Haredi, fewer than 500 evaders have been arrested in 2026. Netanyahu argues against arrests , saying they discourage men from enlisting without coercion.

In July 2026, at the urging of Haredi parties, the government passed a law to temporarily prevent arresting draft evaders. Some members of Netanyahu’s governing coalition opposed the law, however, and right-wing opposition parties filed petitions to challenge it in court .

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett – leader of the Together alliance, and seen as a key contender to oust Netanyahu – has threatened to cut subsidies to the Haredi community if they continue to defy the draft. Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the centrist Yashar party, is another top contender to replace Netanyahu . He has proposed allowing 3% of Haredi men exemptions to study , while drafting the majority.

As the number of conflict zones increases – Gaza, southern Lebanon and Iran, as well as deployments in the West Bank – the unequal burden of military participation is a growing source of resentment among many conscripted Israelis and their families. Seven in 10 Jewish Israelis favor drafting the Haredim.
Shas and UTJ, however, have declared they will not join a coalition unless it promises to codify the draft exemption into law .

When the Haredi parties exited Netanyahu’s coalition, Likud replaced them with nationalist parties that emphasize the state and Jewish supremacy. Particularly notable was the decision to include the Jewish Power party , an offshoot of an earlier group banned for racism ; including Kahanist groups was long seen as a red line .

Haredi communities, on the other hand, tend to prioritize religious Jewishness over the state. Most Haredim do not consider themselves Zionist , and a small percentage are anti-Zionist . They argue that it was sacrilegious for people to create a state of Israel rather than waiting for God to return Jews to the land of Israel. Where nationalist politicians emphasize the secular state and military service, Haredim see their religious study as service to the Jewish community.

As Likud’s changing coalition shows, Netanyahu’s alliances are strategic rather than ideological. I believe his decision to side with the Haredim on the recent draft legislation suggests his coalition is open to revision after the October 2026 election.

As the Haredi community grows , its power in the electoral system will become less disproportionate. In a democratic framework, a large social group would deserve proportional representation and influence. As such, the tension between their electoral power, their demands for exemptions and subsidies, and the tolerance of non-Haredi Jews will persist as a political challenge.

articles.title: Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear
articles.author:
<name>Monique Mitchell Turner, Professor of Communication, Michigan State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/monique-mitchell-turner-1321312"/>
paras: On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers watched a little girl counting petals on a flower. Her voice gave way to a man counting down, and then a nuclear blast filled the screen.

The ad ran as a paid spot only once , in support of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s reelection campaign. It never mentioned his opponent, republican Barry Goldwater . The ad played on a fear voters already held, that Goldwater might start a nuclear war . Republicans protested loudly, Democrats pulled the spot, and the uproar got it rebroadcast in full on network news.

I study how emotional appeals persuade, from how viewers’ moods shape their reactions to political ads to how anxiety drives people to seek out , and sometimes fail to absorb, information about threats.
The LBJ “Daisy” ad shows why political campaigns to this day continue to reach for fear , and it hints at why the payoff is less predictable than you might think.
Fear is an alarm . It tells you something threatening is close. You feel scared when you believe you are at risk from something dangerous that can hurt you.
Anxiety knocks people off autopilot, sharpens attention and sends them looking for new information. That heightened attentiveness may be exactly what a struggling campaign wants.

When political scientists Travis Ridout and Kathleen Searles tracked Senate ads from 2004, they found that front-runners often leaned on enthusiasm and pride in their messaging, while candidates who were behind leaned on fear and anger.

During the 1998 Massachusetts governor’s race, political scientist Ted Brader ran a study that embedded campaign ads in a news broadcast and changed only the music and images, keeping the words identical . Those changes produced completely different reactions. When a negative ad paired grainy black-and-white images of drug use with tense music, viewers paid closer attention to the spoken message and became more open to reconsidering their chosen candidate.

Fear cues – like a nuclear mushroom cloud – can push viewers to weigh fresh information and reconsider their choice. One surprise: Politically informed citizens were more responsive to these emotional cues than less engaged ones. Fear is not simply a tool for swaying the uninformed, undecided voter. It also reaches people who follow politics closely. Emotion provides the motivation, while knowledge provides the ability to think carefully about the issues and positions and seek out more information.

More broadly, a meta-analysis of over 100 studies found that fear appeals reliably shift attitudes and behavior across health and other domains. For instance, public health researcher Lucy Popova tested fear-based messages designed to discourage smokers from trying snus, a smokeless tobacco product. She found that when participants perceived a serious threat but also felt capable of acting on it, they held less favorable attitudes toward snus and were less inclined to try it.

Political attack ads – fear messaging being one type – have a shakier record. A review of more than 100 studies found no dependable evidence that negative campaigning wins elections, and some evidence that it lowers positive feelings toward the candidate who sponsors it.

Communication scholar Kim Witte’s research found that fear motivates action when people believe there is a workable response that they can carry out. When the threat feels big and the solution feels out of reach, people protect themselves from the message instead . They tune out, deny the threat or decide the messenger is the problem.

For example, picture an ad geared toward adolescent vaping that shows teens in hospital beds with ventilators using scary terms like “popcorn lungs.” If the ad also communicates that vaping can destroy lungs irreversibly, the teen audience is likely to experience extreme fear while at the same time feeling like there’s no way to fix the problem.

My colleagues and I have seen this effect in our own experiments. We found that people who felt highly anxious and also confident they could act sought out the most information . Those who felt anxious but lacked that confidence did go looking, yet they recalled very little. Anxiety pushed them to search but got in the way of absorbing what they read.
A campaign that frightens voters without offering a clear step to address the issue could end up producing plenty of anxious attention and very little learning.

Empowerment also helps explain who shows up at the polls. Political scientist Nicholas Valentino and colleagues found that anger boosted voter participation more reliably than anxiety, and anxiety mattered mainly for people who already had the skills and resources to take actions like donate to campaigns, attend rallies, sign petitions and so on.
Fear does its most reliable work when it attaches to a stereotype voters already carry. The 1988 presidential race provides two classic examples.

One controversial ad, produced in support of Republican George H.W. Bush, showed a mugshot of a Black man. The ad named the man, Willie Horton, and a voiceover explained that he’d committed rape and assault while on a weekend furlough from prison as part of a program run under Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis, the Democratic candidate. The spot linked fears about crime to race without saying so directly.

Bush’s campaign followed up with the “ Revolving Door ” ad, which built on that anxiety. It featured stark, black-and-white footage of inmates marching through a revolving gate while a narrator warned that Dukakis had let murderers out of prison on weekend passes.

Political scientist Tali Mendelberg’s research described in “ The Race Card ” shows that these implicit appeals to prejudices and fears are powerful . But they lose much of their force once someone publicly names them as racial. Implicit appeals work because they slip past most voters’ commitment to racial equality; once the racial message is pointed out, voters recognize it and many reject it rather than see themselves as endorsing prejudice.

In a national experiment, Public Policy researcher Mirya Holman and colleagues found that when campaign messages triggered fears of terrorism , voters turned to their stereotypes of strong leaders as masculine. Those stereotypes hurt a female Democratic candidate, while Republican candidates of either gender were unaffected, since Republicans are already seen as tough on security .

A message communicating a threat does not need to name a candidate’s identity to disadvantage them. It simply makes voters reach for the stereotypes they already hold. There’s less systematic research on candidates’ religion, though the same mechanism – fear pushing voters to rely on the stereotypes they already hold about who can keep them safe – predicts similar vulnerability for Muslim candidates .
Using fear as a campaign tool is nothing new.

In 1828, opponents accused presidential candidate Andrew Jackson of murder and cannibalism . Both parties have leaned on fear in the television era, from Reagan’s 1984 “ Bear ” ad about an unnamed Soviet threat, to Democrats’ 1996 warnings that seniors’ Medicare was at risk .

What has grown is negativity overall. Political scientist John Geer’s analysis of presidential ads from 1960 to 2004 documents that rise , though he also found attack ads, more likely than positive ones, to focus on real issues rather than personal traits. The evidence that fear specifically has increased, as opposed to negativity in general, is less clear.

The current media landscape shifts this dynamic significantly; while traditional nightly news broadcasts have seen a decline in viewership, targeted social media feeds have become the emotional battleground.

Recent digital campaign data shows that negative ads are highly prized online because they successfully grab attention by provoking strong emotions like fear and anger. Because platform recommendation systems are heavily driven by user activity , campaigns are incentivized to use emotionally charged appeals to maximize viral engagement across feeds.

Fear works less like a switch and more like a spotlight. It grabs attention and opens minds to change, but whether that turns into a vote, a boycott of the ballot box or resentment toward the messenger depends on what comes next.

articles.title: I expect you to cry: what the James Bond actors may face at the final audition
articles.author: Stuart Heritage
paras: Jack Lowden, Callum Turner and Josh O’Connor are rumoured to be the final candidates taking screentests this weekend. So how can they best prepare? And who is likely to triumph?

This weekend, the identity of the next James Bond is finally expected to be known – to the insiders, at least. According to reports, a number of youngish British actors – definitely three, possibly five – will have their final screen tests.

To say it has been a long time coming is an understatement. It is five years since Daniel Craig was killed in a hail of missiles at the end of No Time to Die, and in that time – even long before it – a swarm of actors have been tipped to replace him, only to age out of the role due to a combination of indecisiveness and cutthroat backstage corporate shenanigans. Whoever is declared to be 007 will be joining the franchise after what is likely to be the longest fallow period in the franchise’s 64-year history.

articles.title: America must reverse Trump’s moral squalor | Robert Reich

paras: The president shows a unique disregard for the opinions, norms and ideals of the nation – and, for that matter, humanity

The Democrats’ focus on affordability seems to be a winning strategy (we’ll know for sure in a little over two weeks). But we mustn’t lose sight of the moral squalor at the core of the Trump regime and the necessity of ending it.

It’s that moral squalor – the utter disregard for the opinions, norms and ideals of the nation and, for that matter, of humanity – that uniquely marks Trump and the reprobates he has attracted to Washington. It has also poisoned much of the Republican party, including the billionaires and tech bros who finance it.
